title: Working From Home Made You an Hour Lonelier Every Day. A Half-Million-Person Study Just Proved It.
excerpt: Remote workers in 'remotable' jobs — overwhelmingly in tech — spend an extra hour alone each workday and don't make up for it after hours. For South Asian professionals 10,000 miles from family, the numbers hit differently.
body:
The workplace is one of the primary places where adults form and maintain friendships. A landmark study published in the journal *Science* on June 4 analysed data from more than 500,000 American workers surveyed between 2011 and 2024, and found that remote work is making people measurably lonelier — and that the isolation is damaging their mental health.

The findings are especially relevant for the Indian diaspora, which is disproportionately concentrated in the technology sector — exactly the kind of "remotable" jobs the study examined.

## One Extra Hour Alone, Every Workday

Researchers from the University of Virginia, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and other institutions compared two groups: workers in jobs that could shift to remote work after the pandemic (software engineering, data analysis, consulting) and those in jobs requiring physical presence (nursing, cooking, construction). They excluded the peak pandemic years of 2020 and 2021 to isolate the effects of remote work itself.

The results were stark. Workers in remote-friendly jobs spent roughly one extra hour alone each workday compared to their in-person peers. Critically, they did not compensate after hours. "We even see a decrease in spending time with friends after the workday relative to people in non-remotable occupations," said lead author Natalia Emanuel, an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

People who lived alone were hit hardest. Their pandemic-prompted increase in days spent completely alone was ten times that of people living with others. Some individuals had days with "no human contact at all," Emanuel told NPR. "Not even like a wave to a barista, not somebody also checking for ripeness of the avocados at the grocery store."

## The Mental Health Cost Is Not Subtle

The isolation was not merely uncomfortable — it was clinically measurable. Compared to workers in non-remotable jobs, those who could work from home reported higher rates of mental distress, were more likely to see a mental health professional, and filled more prescriptions for depression and anxiety medications.

"We actually see the entire distribution shifting to more distress," Emanuel told *Science News*. The authors estimate that the rise of remote work explains roughly a third of the national increase in mental distress during the period they studied.

The findings echo what former US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy warned in 2023 when he declared an epidemic of loneliness and isolation, noting that social disconnection raises the risk of depression, anxiety, and earlier death. A widely cited earlier study found that being socially disconnected is as harmful to health as smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.

## Why This Hits the Diaspora Harder

In the United States, Indian-origin workers are among the most heavily represented in precisely the technology, consulting, and finance roles that the study categorises as "remotable." The H-1B visa pipeline channels hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals into software engineering, IT services, and data roles at companies that have largely shifted to hybrid or fully remote arrangements since the pandemic.

For these workers, the isolation documented in the *Science* study compounds an existing deficit. Most Indian professionals in the US live thousands of miles from extended family. The joint-family social infrastructure that serves as a mental health buffer in India — grandparents, aunts, cousins, childhood friends within visiting distance — simply does not exist in most American suburbs. Remote work removes the one reliable social anchor many of them had: the office.

The cultural dimension makes it worse. Mental health remains deeply stigmatised in many South Asian families and communities. A 2023 survey by the South Asian Public Health Association found that over 60% of South Asian Americans had never spoken to a mental health professional, and nearly half cited family stigma as a barrier. When remote work quietly increases anxiety and depression, the cultural reluctance to seek help means the suffering often goes unaddressed.

## Hybrid Is Not a Silver Bullet, but Choice Helps

The study's authors were careful to note that their findings do not justify blunt return-to-office mandates. "Our results are not saying that there are no benefits of remote work," co-author Emma Harrington, an economist at the University of Virginia, told *Scientific American*. Remote work saves commuting time and money, allows more time with immediate family, and makes workplaces more accessible to individuals with disabilities.

Stanford economist Nicholas Bloom, who was not involved in the study, pointed to a more nuanced path. Past research suggests that "the best way to improve mental health with [work from home] is: let people choose," he told *Scientific American*. More than half of remote employees in the US already work hybrid schedules, averaging about 2.3 days in the office per week, according to Gallup data.

For Indian professionals navigating the tension between flexibility and connection, the study offers a data-backed nudge: the convenience of the home office comes with a real cost, and it is worth actively building social structures outside the workday. Community gatherings, temple events, neighbourhood walks, even regular video calls with family back home — these are not luxuries. The research suggests they are, quite literally, mental health interventions.

## What You Can Do This Week

The *Science* study did not track whether people eventually adapted to remote isolation by building new social ties. That gap in the data is, in its own way, an invitation: the adaptation is not automatic, but it is possible.

If you work remotely and recognise the slow creep of isolation — fewer spontaneous conversations, fewer reasons to leave the house, an inbox that has replaced most of your human contact — the evidence says the risk is real and measurable. The fix does not require an office mandate. It requires deliberate social investment: joining a community group, scheduling a weekly chai with a friend, or simply choosing to work from a café twice a week instead of the spare bedroom.

For a community that already carries the weight of distance from home, that investment may be the most important health decision of the year.
